chunks.title: Project and company scope
chunks.text: BrandScope is an independent portfolio project inspired by a P&G brand management role. It is not P&G employment, a commissioned campaign, an endorsement, or a production retailer integration. No project can guarantee recruitment or prove language proficiency.

chunks.title: Swedish sample and localization
chunks.text: Sweden has eight identified shoppers and 34 purchase orders from a historical UK retailer. Swedish net merchandise sales are GBP 35,166.41. This is too small and unrepresentative for a national Swedish FMCG market estimate. Currency remains GBP. Swedish copy is a draft requiring native review.

chunks.title: Sales and returns reconciliation
chunks.text: Historical gross merchandise sales are GBP 10,229,905.15; recorded returns are GBP 475,248.66; net sales are GBP 9,754,656.49. These are source dataset totals, not revenue generated by BrandScope.

chunks.title: Dataset size, cleaning and license
chunks.text: The source has 541,909 rows. Exact deduplication removes 5,268; merchandise and validity rules exclude another 5,857; 530,784 rows remain. Missing-ID sales remain in totals, but shopper analytics exclude them. UCI Online Retail by Chen (2015), DOI 10.24432/C5BW33, is licensed CC BY 4.0.

chunks.title: Machine learning model results and repurchase benchmark
chunks.text: Supervised machine learning results: the selected random forest predicts a purchase within 30 days. On the November holdout, average precision is 0.6367, ROC-AUC 0.7356, and top-20% precision 0.6776. Purchase propensity is not causal offer response, churn probability, or guaranteed profit.

chunks.title: Temporal leakage prevention
chunks.text: Supervised training uses March–August customer snapshots with future 30-day labels. September selects the model, October fits sigmoid calibration, and November is the final report month. Features use strictly earlier transactions. Customers can recur across snapshots; the evaluation is temporal, not customer-disjoint.

chunks.title: Calibration limitations
chunks.text: October sigmoid calibration is frozen before November reporting. November calibrated Brier score is about 0.1870 versus 0.1860 for the raw forest; calibration did not improve that metric. Reliability bins and feature-drift diagnostics show remaining uncertainty. Do not describe these probabilities as reliably calibrated in production.

chunks.title: Product recommendation evidence
chunks.text: A 32-factor TruncatedSVD recommender learns co-purchase structure from pre-cutoff purchase histories. November hit-rate@5 is 27.91% versus 14.43% for popularity. Mean recall@5 is only 3.20%. The eligible population is known shoppers with at least one novel future product, not all shoppers. Basket-seed inference differs from full-history evaluation.

chunks.title: Why discounts can destroy campaign profit
chunks.text: The planning sandbox includes discounts on purchases that would have happened without marketing. With 2,000 shoppers, 5% baseline conversion, assumed 3 percentage-point gain, GBP 45 order value, 45% margin and GBP 600 cost, a 5% discount gives GBP 255 modelled contribution; 20% discount gives GBP -825. These are assumptions, not realized results.

chunks.title: Sample size and power
chunks.text: The default conversion test needs about 1,059 people per arm, exceeding a total audience of 2,000. This normal approximation uses two-sided alpha 0.05 and 80% power. The primary contribution outcome needs its own variance-based design. A positive commercial scenario does not imply a sufficiently powered test.

chunks.title: Uplift and causal marketing
chunks.text: This retail dataset contains no randomized treatment assignment or advertising exposure. A purchase predictor cannot identify who would buy only because of an offer. Uplift modeling, causal campaign ROI and marketing mix modeling require suitable additional data. BrandScope does not fabricate treatment labels or channel spend.

chunks.title: Analyze randomized experiment results
chunks.text: Experiment lab accepts one row per assigned participant: participant_id, arm (control/treatment), converted (0/1), contribution (GBP). Include nonconverters and all costs. It reports contribution difference, approximate 95% intervals, secondary conversion difference and a 50:50 sample-ratio mismatch check. Duplicate participants are rejected. Synthetic demo results do not constitute a real campaign.

chunks.title: How the evidence assistant works
chunks.text: The evidence assistant uses a fitted TF-IDF index to retrieve project passages, show source links and abstain when token similarity is insufficient. It is retrieval NLP, not a generative language model or live internet search. Similarity is not a probability of correctness. It does not send questions to an external provider.

chunks.title: Live events and hosting boundary
chunks.text: The local Python app accepts validated HTTP events, deduplicates event IDs, stores them in SQLite and refreshes every two seconds. GitHub Pages uses browser-local event storage. Demonstration events are synthetic and never change historical retail metrics. No existing retailer feed is connected.

chunks.title: RFM shopper segmentation
chunks.text: RFM means recency, frequency and monetary value. Champions have recency at most 30 days and at least three orders; high-value at-risk shoppers have recency above 90 days and top-quartile gross spend. There are five mutually exclusive rules. The all-history at-risk group contains 96 shoppers and about GBP 428k of past gross purchases; this is not recoverable value.

chunks.title: Marketing strategy and next action
chunks.text: Use shopper evidence to choose an audience and a relevant proposition, review consent and wholesale status, model contribution, then run a pre-registered test. Consumer interviews, retailer availability, actual margins and native Swedish review are still needed before activation. Scale only with trustworthy contribution evidence and acceptable guardrails.

chunks.title: Cleaning and audit
chunks.text: 1. Download the original UCI Online Retail ZIP and record SHA-256. 2. Read the entire workbook without sampling. 3. Drop exact duplicated rows across all original columns (5,268). 4. Keep merchandise codes matching five digits plus an optional letter, nonmissing description, strictly positive unit price and nonzero quantity. This removes 5,857 rows after deduplication, including non-merchandise charges/adjustments and invalid rows. This is a declared scope filter, not a universal retail cleaning rule. 5. Convert unit price to integer pence with round-to-nearest; multiply by quantity. Positive and negative merchandise quantities are retained (522,121 positive, 8,663 negative). 6. Preserve missing customer IDs in sales totals (131,424 retained rows); omit them from customer analytics.

chunks.title: Cleaning and audit
chunks.text: Audit identity: 541,909 = 5,268 + 5,857 + 530,784. Duplicate removal assumes identical repeated records are accidental duplicates; the dataset lacks a unique line ID, so that choice could remove legitimate identical line items. Negative merchandise rows are treated as recorded returns, not audited physical returns. Invoice cancellation flags and negative quantities are not independently reconciled to original orders. Outliers are retained; unusually large wholesale orders can dominate averages.

chunks.title: Segment precedence
chunks.text: 1. Champions: recency ≤ 30 days and frequency ≥ 3. 2. At risk · high value: recency > 90 days and monetary ≥ the 75th percentile within selected market/window. 3. Loyal shoppers: recency ≤ 90 and frequency ≥ 2. 4. New shoppers: recency ≤ 30 and frequency = 1. 5. Reactivation pool: all remaining identified shoppers. This label can include recent moderate-frequency shoppers as well as inactive shoppers; review row-level eligibility before activation.

chunks.title: Segment precedence
chunks.text: These are business rules, not learned clusters or calibrated churn scores. Market/window selection recomputes segment membership and high-value thresholds. The last-90-days view cannot observe earlier purchases, so “new” means new within that window and cohort acquisition may be left-truncated.

chunks.title: Cohorts and baskets
chunks.text: First observed purchase month in selected data defines cohort. M0 is 100%; Mk is unique purchasing shoppers at calendar month k / cohort size. Future months are null; incomplete observed months remain observed and can depress retention. No censoring correction is applied.

chunks.title: Cohorts and baskets
chunks.text: Product pairs are counted once per invoice among the 35 most frequently ordered products. The support denominator is all positive purchase invoices in the selected market/window, including invoices containing none of those top products. Joint-basket minimum = five. Both directions are considered; report the eight highest association-lift rules. Support = joint baskets / all purchase orders; confidence A→B = joint baskets / baskets containing A; association lift = joint baskets × all purchase orders / (baskets containing A × baskets containing B). No Apriori efficiency claim, no hypothesis-testing correction and no causal interpretation.

chunks.title: Historical evaluation
chunks.text: At 1 Aug, 1 Sep and 1 Oct 2011, compute customer features strictly before the cutoff. Rank by mean(percentile frequency, percentile monetary, 1 − percentile recency); resolve ties by CustomerID. Select floor(20% × eligible) customers. Label whether each purchased in the following 30 days. Compare precision to the overall repurchase prevalence and the top-20% monetary-only ranker. Features never include post-cutoff records. Cleaning happens before splitting; exact duplicate removal uses all source rows but does not tune features or labels.

chunks.title: Historical evaluation
chunks.text: The same customers can appear across windows. There are only three descriptive checks, without confidence intervals or an external dataset. No threshold was optimized using these results, but future performance and causal response remain unestablished. “Ranking lift” is precision / overall repurchase rate; it is not incremental conversion, profit uplift, model accuracy, or a randomized treatment effect.

chunks.title: Campaign economics
chunks.text: All inputs are assumptions. Let N = rollout audience, b = baseline conversion, l = absolute conversion gain, A = pre-discount order value, m = contribution margin before discount, d = discount fraction on all treatment orders, C = additional campaign cost.

chunks.title: Campaign economics
chunks.text: Baseline contribution = N b A m. Campaign contribution = N (b+l) A (m−d) − C. Their difference = N A [l m − (b+l)d] − C.

chunks.title: Campaign economics
chunks.text: Break-even l = [C + N A b d] / [N A(m−d)] when denominator > 0. No finite positive break-even is shown when margin ≤ discount. Inputs must satisfy b+l ≤ 1. Break-even above the feasible conversion gain should also be treated as commercially unattainable.

chunks.title: Campaign economics
chunks.text: Conversion sample size uses an equal-arm, two-proportion normal approximation with 80% power and two-sided alpha .05. It is a planning approximation; extreme rates/small samples, clustering, attrition and repeated testing require a different design. It does not power contribution, whose variance is unavailable. No test results or significance claims are fabricated.

chunks.title: Runtime boundary
chunks.text: The static app uses bundled aggregate JSON and browser localStorage for simulated events/scenarios. The Python app uses SQLite for actual HTTP ingestion and scenario persistence. The monitor polls every two seconds; it is near-real-time polling, not an SSE/WebSocket implementation. Events carry explicit synthetic flags and never mutate historical analyses. The server is a loopback demonstration service, not a production multi-user system.

chunks.title: BrandScope — strategy and activation brief
chunks.text: Independent portfolio case study inspired by the supplied P&G Brand Management Summer Internship 2027 description (Stockholm, R000159972). No employment, sponsorship, endorsement or access to P&G systems is implied.

chunks.title: Executive decision
chunks.text: Prioritize a small, measurable shopper reactivation test over indiscriminate discounting. Valuable inactive shoppers are a hypothesis-generating audience, not guaranteed recoverable revenue. Separate the historical gift-retail evidence from a future Swedish consumer-goods application.

chunks.title: Executive decision
chunks.text: Across the full cleaned merchandise dataset, 96 shoppers meet the selected high-value-at-risk rule. Their historical gross purchases total about £428k. This is past spend, not addressable annual sales, current demand, customer lifetime value, or expected campaign impact. The default 2,000-person campaign sandbox is an independent planning scenario and is not this 96-person audience. A 96-person audience is generally too small for a modest conversion experiment; the studio should expose that constraint.

chunks.title: Marketing choices
chunks.text: Audience: Use segment rules to define and audit eligible shoppers. Exclude nonconsented contacts and identify wholesale accounts before a consumer campaign. This application does not store contact data or send messages.

chunks.title: Marketing choices
chunks.text: Proposition: Helpful product relevance and a thoughtful reminder. Avoid unsubstantiated superiority, sustainability or performance claims. The dataset cannot establish why shoppers stopped buying.

chunks.title: Marketing choices
chunks.text: Product: Test a complementary pairing supported by repeated baskets. Association evidence supports an experiment, not an automatic recommendation rollout. Check availability and category suitability.

chunks.title: Marketing choices
chunks.text: Price: Start with relevance at full price as the comparator to an offer. Include discounts paid on purchases that would have happened anyway. The contribution planner makes this cannibalization visible.

chunks.title: Marketing choices
chunks.text: Place: CRM is a proposed low-cost test channel if consent and reachability exist. Retail media or social activation requires platform exposure data, budget planning and permission; none is fabricated here.

chunks.title: Marketing choices
chunks.text: Promotion: Two messages with the same audience, timing and offer; vary one decision at a time where possible. A drafted Swedish line is included to demonstrate localization workflow and requires native review. It does not prove the author's business-language proficiency.

chunks.title: Measurement and experiment brief
chunks.text: - Business goal: profitable repeat purchase, assessed by incremental contribution per eligible shopper. - Assignment: eligible shoppers randomized once, 50:50 treatment versus no-message control. Record assignment before exposure; analyze by original assignment. - Outcome window: predeclare 30 days, with a return-observation policy to avoid early profit claims. - Primary metric: contribution per eligible shopper, including product, fulfilment, incentive and campaign costs. - Secondary metric: purchase conversion; the studio provides an approximate conversion power calculation only. - Guardrails: opt-outs, complaints, returns, data freshness and delivery failure. No numerical safety thresholds are invented as company policy. - Analysis: uncertainty intervals, randomization integrity, missing outcomes, contamination and wholesale/consumer differences. Use a pilot to estimate contribution variance before sizing the primary metric. - Scale criterion: positive incremental contribution supported by uncertainty and acceptable agreed guardrails. A positive spreadsheet scenario alone cannot satisfy it.

chunks.title: Default sandbox worked example
chunks.text: Planning assumptions: 2,000 eligible shoppers; baseline conversion 5%; absolute conversion gain 3 percentage points; pre-discount order value £45; contribution margin 45%; 5% discount on all treatment orders; £600 extra campaign cost.

chunks.title: Default sandbox worked example
chunks.text: - Baseline contribution: 2,000 × 0.05 × £45 × 0.45 = £2,025. - Treatment contribution: 2,000 × 0.08 × £45 × (0.45 − 0.05) − £600 = £2,280. - Modelled incremental contribution: £255, not realized profit. - Incremental orders: 60; incremental pre-discount gross revenue: £2,700. - Break-even absolute conversion gain: 2.29 percentage points.

chunks.title: Default sandbox worked example
chunks.text: The available audience check uses an approximate equal-arm conversion test. Monetary outcomes need their own sample-size design. The historical dataset has no campaign exposures and cannot validate these assumed conversion rates or margins.

chunks.title: Proposed 10-week delivery plan
chunks.text: This is a prospective plan aligned to the internship's working style, not a claim of ten weeks already completed.

chunks.title: English stakeholder summary
chunks.text: “The historical analysis identifies an audience worth investigating, rather than proving demand. I would first validate consent, wholesale status and message relevance. I would then test contribution against a control, including the cost of discounts on baseline purchases. The Swedish sample is too small to justify a national recommendation.”

chunks.title: Swedish stakeholder summary — draft for review
chunks.text: “Den historiska analysen pekar ut en målgrupp som är värd att undersöka, men bevisar inte efterfrågan. Nästa steg är att kontrollera samtycke, kundtyp och budskapets relevans. Därefter föreslås ett kontrollerat test med fokus på lönsamhet. Det svenska urvalet är för litet för nationella slutsatser.”

chunks.title: BrandScope 2 — model and data label
chunks.text: Independent portfolio research using one licensed historical retailer. No P&G systems, current Swedish FMCG sales, consumer interviews, advertising exposures or randomized treatment labels are present. Predictions do not establish the effect of marketing or guarantee a hiring outcome.

chunks.title: Intended decisions
chunks.text: 1. Repurchase model: demonstrate prioritization of likely purchasers, compare with simpler rankers, and make prediction uncertainty visible. 2. Product discovery: rank novel product candidates using learned co-purchase factors and compare with broad popularity. 3. Evidence assistant: retrieve project source passages without inventing an answer. 4. Experiment lab: analyze supplied fixed-horizon randomized outcomes; this is statistical tooling, not an ML treatment-effect model.

chunks.title: Intended decisions
chunks.text: These are assistive case-study capabilities, not approved automated customer activation or production models.

chunks.title: Data and privacy boundary
chunks.text: The original UCI Online Retail data contains 541,909 transaction rows from a UK gift retailer, 1 December 2010 through 9 December 2011. The declared cleaning pipeline retains 530,784 merchandise rows, including recorded returns. Model features and product factors use positive purchases with known customer IDs. No row-level customer identities, contact details, raw source workbook or local SQLite database are published. Exported model trees contain only aggregate probabilities and thresholds; parity examples contain behavior features without identifiers.

chunks.title: Data and privacy boundary
chunks.text: Scope filters and deduplication are applied before temporal snapshots. No feature or label threshold is optimized on November. Exact duplicate removal assumes identical repeated lines are accidental duplicates; lack of unique source line IDs remains a limitation.

chunks.title: Supervised repurchase model
chunks.text: Target: at least one positive purchase in the 30 days following a snapshot. This is purchase propensity, not explicit churn, offer responsiveness, customer lifetime value, contribution margin or causal uplift.

chunks.title: Supervised repurchase model
chunks.text: Eligible population: identified shoppers with at least one positive purchase before the cutoff. A shopper can recur across monthly snapshots, matching repeated scoring of existing accounts; this is temporal evaluation, not customer-disjoint evaluation. Wholesale accounts are not separately identified.

chunks.title: Supervised repurchase model
chunks.text: Features: days since last purchase; all-history distinct purchase orders; all-history gross positive spend in GBP; days since first purchase; orders in the trailing 30 days; gross spend in the trailing 30 days; distinct products; average order value. Every feature is calculated strictly before its snapshot. No customer identifier, country, future outcome, treatment, or post-cutoff transaction is an input. All features use log(1+x). Logistic regression additionally uses scaling fitted only on training rows.

chunks.title: Supervised repurchase model
chunks.text: Two fixed candidates are compared: logistic regression (C=1, scaled log features) and random forest (120 trees, max depth 7, min leaf 30, 80% feature subsampling). All random seeds are 42. Selection maximizes September average precision, with Brier score as a tie-break. The forest wins narrowly in September (0.59644 vs 0.59478). October fits a sigmoid calibrator to the frozen forest's logit probabilities. The training model is not refitted with calibration/test outcomes.

chunks.title: Final November results
chunks.text: Top 20% contains 794 shoppers. The calibrated forest captures 40.24% of future purchasing shoppers. Average precision is a ranking summary, not classification accuracy. ROC-AUC measures discrimination; top-20% precision is not incremental response.

chunks.title: Final November results
chunks.text: Mixed evidence is retained: logistic regression slightly outperforms the forest on November AP and Brier even though the forest won September selection. Calibration worsens November Brier from 0.18604 to 0.18702 while slightly improving log loss. The app retains the earlier-selected protocol and discloses these results. “Calibration fitted” must not become “well-calibrated production probabilities.”

chunks.title: Final November results
chunks.text: A paired customer bootstrap (500 replicates, seed 42) gives an AP difference versus RFM of 0.03307, percentile 95% interval [0.02212, 0.04404]. This interval conditions on the fixed fitted model and one test month. It does not account for training uncertainty, longitudinal dependence, model search, retailer variation or future time shifts.

chunks.title: Inspection and monitoring
chunks.text: The app shows fixed-seed permutation AP drops on the final holdout and raw forest tree-path probability contributions for a supplied profile. Path contributions decompose changes from each tree's root probability to its leaf before calibration. They are not SHAP values, calibrated probability changes, or causal effects. Correlated inputs complicate both permutation and path interpretation.

chunks.title: Inspection and monitoring
chunks.text: Reliability bins compare mean probability to actual repurchase in November. Coarse population stability indices compare October and November feature distributions. No automatically validated alarm thresholds are claimed. The profile form flags features outside training min/max ranges, but in-range inputs can still be unrepresentative or internally inconsistent.

chunks.title: Inspection and monitoring
chunks.text: Capacity tables compare sums of predictions with observed purchasers at fixed audience fractions. They are historical prioritization diagnostics, not expected offer-induced conversions or permission to spend.

chunks.title: Product factors and recommendations
chunks.text: Fit a user-product sparse matrix of log(1 + distinct purchase invoices per pair), using each training period's top 500 products by invoice count. TruncatedSVD learns product factors without centering the sparse matrix. Compare ranks 16 and 32 with popularity on September mean recall@5 (hit-rate tie-break); 32-factor SVD wins. Refit the chosen factorization on purchases strictly before 1 Nov 2011 and evaluate subsequent 30-day novel purchases. Its fit uses no November outcomes.

chunks.title: Product factors and recommendations
chunks.text: Evaluation population: 1,247 known shoppers who purchase at least one previously unbought product in the November window. The model ranks catalog candidates excluding all their prior products. Novel products outside the fitted catalog remain in the denominator and count as misses. Thus this is not an unconditional conversion or recommendation success rate across all shoppers.

chunks.title: Product factors and recommendations
chunks.text: Only 36.74% of novel target products fall in the top-500 candidate catalog. Low recall and this coverage gap remain visible. Scores are latent ranking scores, not probabilities or sales effects.

chunks.title: Product factors and recommendations
chunks.text: Interactive inference boundary: the browser takes one or two supplied seed products and sums their product vectors to rank candidates. Offline evaluation uses each shopper's full weighted history. This difference means the reported holdout metrics must not be advertised as measured performance of the two-seed interaction. Popularity is displayed as a cold-start fallback; unknown codes are rejected. No product availability, customer need or suitability is inferred.

chunks.title: Evidence retrieval NLP
chunks.text: A fitted English TF-IDF index contains curated factual passages and paragraphs from the project’s methods, strategy, model card and experiment documentation. Query vectors and stored passage vectors use cosine similarity. The assistant returns existing passages with source links and abstains below a declared similarity threshold. It does not call an LLM, generate explanations, access the user's LinkedIn account, browse live sources or send queries to an external provider.

chunks.title: Evidence retrieval NLP
chunks.text: Similarity is not confidence in correctness. Retrieval can return a related but unhelpful passage. The checked example questions are smoke tests, not an independently annotated retrieval benchmark. Multilingual understanding is not claimed. No “RAG with an LLM,” semantic foundation-model embedding or generative AI claim should be made.

chunks.title: Portable inference and reproducibility
chunks.text: The committed JSON contract contains the fitted forest or logistic parameters, sigmoid calibrator, feature ranges, product factors and TF-IDF index. Python and browser JavaScript execute the same contract. Reference cases compare exported predictions to sklearn with tolerance 1e-7. CI executes actual browser-engine code in Node and the Python HTTP integration tests. No pickle/joblib artifact is deserialized in the app.

chunks.title: Portable inference and reproducibility
chunks.text: Rebuild with python scripts/build_data.py, python scripts/train_models.py, python scripts/train_recommender.py, python scripts/build_experiment_demo.py, and python scripts/build_knowledge.py after installing requirements-ml.txt. The source ZIP fingerprint is attached to the supervised benchmark; model-file SHA-256 is recorded in docs/outputs/ml-benchmark.json.

chunks.title: Why no uplift or marketing-mix model is claimed
chunks.text: Purchase logs lack randomized offer assignment, exposure, media spend and observed margins. Adding invented columns would not establish a causal treatment effect. EconML and Meta Robyn are research references for a future authorized dataset, not installed/implemented methods in BrandScope. The experiment analyser supplies the next evidence step without manufacturing a campaign result.

chunks.title: Research sources
chunks.text: - [Scikit-learn probability calibration](https://scikit-learn.org/1.7/modules/calibration.html) - [Scikit-learn TruncatedSVD](https://scikit-learn.org/1.7/modules/generated/sklearn.decomposition.TruncatedSVD.html) - [Scikit-learn permutation feature importance](https://scikit-learn.org/1.7/modules/permutation_importance.html) - [Recommenders project](https://github.com/recommenders-team/recommenders) - [EconML](https://github.com/py-why/EconML) - [Meta Robyn](https://github.com/facebookexperimental/Robyn)

chunks.title: Purpose and input contract
chunks.text: Analyze a predeclared, fixed-horizon, two-arm test with expected allocation 50:50. Upload a CSV or paste records with columns participant_id,arm,converted,contribution. Use one row per originally assigned eligible participant, including nonconverters. Arm must be control or treatment; converted must be 0 or 1; contribution is finite signed GBP after variable costs, incentives, refunds and allocated campaign costs. Duplicate/missing IDs and malformed values are rejected. Maximum 20,000 rows and 2 MB. At least 30 participants in each arm are required for this demonstration's large-sample calculation; this threshold does not guarantee accurate monetary intervals.

chunks.title: Purpose and input contract
chunks.text: The public preview calculates in-browser and does not send CSV content to a server or save it in localStorage. Local mode posts records to the loopback Python API. The demonstration code does not retain participant records in its event database.

chunks.title: Calculations
chunks.text: Primary outcome: difference in mean contribution per assigned participant, treatment minus control. Standard error is the square root of treatment sample variance / treatment n + control sample variance / control n. Report difference ± 1.959964 × standard error as a large-sample approximate 95% interval.

chunks.title: Calculations
chunks.text: Secondary outcome: conversion-rate difference with an unpooled normal-approximation interval. Rare event/non-event counts below ten are flagged. Conversion is not a substitute for profitable contribution.

chunks.title: Calculations
chunks.text: Sample-ratio mismatch: Pearson chi-squared statistic against a 50:50 expected split, one degree of freedom; two-sided imbalance tail computed via erfc(sqrt(chi-squared/2)). p < 0.01 flags an assignment investigation. Passing this check does not prove randomization validity.

chunks.title: Calculations
chunks.text: Decision text first prioritizes a sample-ratio warning. Otherwise, an entirely positive contribution interval suggests positive evidence subject to guardrails, an entirely negative interval flags harm, and an interval crossing zero is inconclusive. This is an analytic aid, not an automatic launch decision.

chunks.title: Explicitly synthetic example
chunks.text: web/models/synthetic-experiment.csv contains 8,000 simulated participants (4,000 per arm), generated with seed 42. It is prominently labelled synthetic in the app. There was no real campaign.

chunks.title: Explicitly synthetic example
chunks.text: Control has 295 conversions (7.375%); treatment has 405 (10.125%). Secondary conversion difference is +2.75 percentage points, approximate interval [1.51, 3.99] pp. However contribution difference is only £0.2291 per participant, approximate interval [−£0.0059, £0.4641], so the primary outcome is inconclusive. This is a deliberate example of conversion evidence not being sufficient to declare profitable growth.

chunks.title: Operational limitations
chunks.text: Independent-participant, large-sample intervals are not suitable for all heavy-tailed monetary outcomes. There is no cluster adjustment, repeated-look/optional-stopping correction, multiplicity adjustment, missing-outcome correction, return-window enforcement or automatic guardrail validation. Obtain appropriate design and statistical review for a real campaign. Include original assignment rather than only reached/converting people, and resolve identity, consent, complete windows and cost definitions upstream.

chunks.title: Reproduce
chunks.text: python scripts/build_experiment_demo.py regenerates the synthetic CSV. experiments.py provides the Python analyser; web/ml-engine.js provides the browser equivalent. CI checks the same reference contribution difference and interval decision in both environments.

scope: English project evidence only; retrieval NLP, not generative AI
